messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to fit a DM model to my dataset, but I am having a tough time finding non-conflicting initial values. I wonder if anyone would like to share some tricks/tips to overcome the dreaded "Node inconsistent with parents" error. I am starting to think that it is impossible to fit this model to my data.

So far, I have...
Tried initial values proposed in AHM2 book (with many combinations of these).
Increased lambda upper and lower bounds ( lambda = runif(1, 50, 300)) (Bellier pers. com.).
Left-truncate the estimated pop size in the state process with the maximum observed count as proposed in the IPM book (p. 147):
N[i, t] ~ dsum( S[i, t] + R[i, t]) T(maxC[i, t] , ) #--- providing maxC as data
What is your strategy to fit DM models?

Thanks in advance,

Alejandro

Hi Alejandro,

I don't know what are the examples in AHM2 but this has worked for me:

N1 <- Rinit <- Sinit <- apply(Y, c(1,2), max) + 3   # assuming that your counts Y are in [i,t,j] dimensions

for (i in 1:S){
  for(t in 2:T){
    Rinit[i,t] <- rbinom(1,N1[i,t-1],.5) # keep ~half individuals
    Sinit[i,t] <-  ifelse((N1[i,j]-Sinit[i,j])>0, (N1[i,j]-Sinit[i,j]), 0)
}}

N1[,2:T] <- NA

inits <- function(){list(.....,N1,Rinit,Sinit)}

Regards,
Ismael V. Brack

messages.subject: Re: AHMbook package not on CRAN (temporarily we hope)
messages.subject_clean: AHMbook package not on CRAN (temporarily we hope)
messages.body_plain:
The randomFields package is still not back on CRAN, the new versions of randomFields and randomFieldsUtils having been stuck in the CRAN incoming area since 5 May. The new version of AHMbook is waiting in the CRAN incoming area until randomFields reappears. I guess at some point we may have to give up on randomFields and do a version of AHMbook which doesn't use it, but that will not be able to reproduce all the simulations in the books. I am still hoping!

Meanwhile version 2.6.0 is available on GitHub:  remotes::install_github("mikemeredith/AHMbook")

On Saturday, May 7, 2022 at 2:32:51 AM UTC+1 Mike Meredith wrote:
> The AHMbook package was removed from CRAN on 4 May 2022. It uses functions in the RandomFields package for several of the spatial data simulations, and RandomFields was removed because it failed CRAN checks.
>
> If you already have AHMbook and RandomFields on your computer, they will continue to work (unless you are running Fedora).
>
> A new version of RandomFields (3.3.18) has been submitted to CRAN, so if all goes well it will reappear on CRAN in the next few days.
>
> This is the second time RandomFields has caused problems, so the next version of AHMbook (0.2.6) will check to see if RandomFields is available, and if not will try to use functions in the fields package instead. This has already been submitted to CRAN.
>
> If you need to install AHMbook in the meantime, you can use
> remotes::install_github("mikemeredith/AHMbook")
>
> The fields package cannot cope with large field sizes or high correlations, and many of the examples in the book will not work. In particular, it cannot create the data set analyzed in AHM2 section 9.6.1.2. An example data set is now included in the package as simDynoccSpatialData.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am working on an IPM for caribou that uses multiple data types with very unequal distributions of sampling (eg timing and numbers of years). Rather than estimating demographic parameters from raw data within the model I am using estimates and standard errors of the data. The model has two sexes and three age classes (calves, sub-adults, adults). Sub-adults and adults are assumed to have the same survival rates).

I am getting estimates for most parameters, including reproduction (the % of adult cows who breed) and survival. What is odd is that I only get values for abundance for the first few years at best (or just the starting year values at worst) and then everything after that is NaN.

I have attached the script here if anyone wants to take a look, but the state-spaced process model part of it is below. I am getting estimates for all values of Repr, and survival for both sexes/ages (sAf, sAm, sJf, sJm). I cannot understand why I'd be getting NaNs for the relevant abundance values.

  for(yr in 2:nYear){
    # Calves (reproduction)
    nReps[yr] ~ dpois(nAf[yr-1] * Repr[yr])
    nJf[yr] <- nReps[yr] / 2
    nJm[yr] <- nReps[yr] / 2

    # Sub-adults (1-2yrs)
    nYf[yr] ~ dbin(sJf[yr-1], nJf[yr-1])
    nYm[yr] ~ dbin(sJm[yr-1], nJm[yr-1])

    # Adults (≥2yrs)
    nAf[yr] ~ dbin(sAf[yr-1], (nYf[yr-1] + nAf[yr-1]))
    nAm[yr] ~ dbin(sAm[yr-1], (nYm[yr-1] + nAm[yr-1]))

    #  Calculate totals in each year
    totC[yr] <- nJm[yr] + nJf[yr]
    totF[yr] <- nYf[yr] + nAf[yr]
    totM[yr] <- nYm[yr] + nAm[yr]
    totN[yr] <- totF[yr] + totM[yr] + totC[yr]
  }

thanks in advance!
Ben

Hi Ben,
I suspect the MCMC sampler is exploring a portion of parameter space where the population is being driven to "virtual extinction" and there's something like dbin(0,0) being evaluated.  I haven't done these types of model in jags, but it is usually a good strategy to include some sort of minimum bound on abundance values.  For instance, if there are caribou harvests, you might set N_{a,t} = h_{a,t} + NH_{a,t} where the a and t denote age and time, h is the number harvested during the next year (set to a known constant) and NH represents those that aren't harvested.  Alternatively, are there other minimum bounds that could be put in for abundance-at-age?

Cheers, Paul

Hi Paul,

That sounds like a good possibility. I think one of the big issues is the recruitment part of the state-space model.

# Calves (reproduction)

    nReps[yr] ~ dpois(nAf[yr] * Repr[yr])

# Adults (≥2yrs)

    nAf[yr] ~ dbin(sAf[yr-1], (nYf[yr-1] + nAf[yr-1]))

what I cant understand is if I have values for sAf, nYf and nAf in, for example yr=3, why I would end up with an MCMC going out of wack. Would better priors help that? Oh, and if it makes any difference I am doing this in NIMBLE not JAGs.

Hi Ben,

I suspect the MCMC sampler is exploring a portion of parameter space where the population is being driven to "virtual extinction" and there's something like dbin(0,0) being evaluated.  I haven't done these types of model in jags, but it is usually a good strategy to include some sort of minimum bound on abundance values.  For instance, if there are caribou harvests, you might set N_{a,t} = h_{a,t} + NH_{a,t} where the a and t denote age and time, h is the number harvested during the next year (set to a known constant) and NH represents those that aren't harvested.  Alternatively, are there other minimum bounds that could be put in for abundance-at-age?

Cheers, Paul

Betreff: Data augmentation in spatial distance sampling

​Hi all,

I’m playing with the Bayesian spatial distance sampling models from Chapter 9.8 of the first AHM book. However, with my data the models mix poorly and run very slow. I therefore tried a model without data augmentation which runs much faster and mixes way better.

Is there a theoretical reason why I should go with data augmentation? I always assumed that I should do DA because the book tells me so:) But at the moment I think that as long as I don’t want to model individual based effects, the two models should yield similar results. What are your impressions or experiences?

Models

The main idea behind the models in 9.8 is that for each pixel one calculates an expected abundance (lambdag). In a second step one distributes M animals (observed and augmented ones) to the pixels. Each hypothetical animal that exists (zi=1) can either be detected or not with a probability pi calculated from a detection model based on the distance.

Out of curiosity I wrote a model which works without DA. For each pixel g I calculate an expected abundance lambdag. The number of animals on that pixel is then a realization of a Poisson random variable (Nppixg). The number of animals that are observed then follows a binomial distribution with a probability depending on the distance and n = Nppixg.

Simulations

I compared the two models with simulated data. The estimates for sigma (parameter of detection model), beta (influence of habitat on abundance) and N (total abundance) are comparable across 50 runs, see plots. The files for the two models are attached: sim8.txt is the one with DA, sim8_4.txt the new parametrization.

Thanks a lot for any advice!

Cheers,

Sven

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working on an integrated population model for a population with fairly limited data. I am using estimates for survival, age/sex class ratios, and counts along with associated SEs in the model rather than raw data. Over 25 years I have 24 years of data for the best case, and as little as 5 in other cases.

Earlier, I had been getting NaNs for a lot of parameters, but I was able to sort that out by specifying initial values for all parameters (thanks to this group for the advice on that). But now, I am getting posterior estimates with no variance (chains are flat), or very poor mixing with odd looking chains and occasionally bi (or even tri-) modal distribution of posteriors. I've included an example of a few traceplots. My hunch is that this is because of the lack of data, but I should be able to work around that. I would really appreciate some advice or thoughts if anyone has ideas! I am happy to provide code if that would help.

Thanks in advance!
Ben Padilla
